lesson.subtitle: Lesson 8 -- Explaining Brazil: Your Country in Somebody Else's Language
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Laís Paludetto Rodrigues | Lesson 8 -- Explaining Brazil

listenings.text: Before you go, a quick word about the culture fair in November. Every international student gets a table, and the table is the easy part. What I want you to prepare is five minutes of talking. Not a lecture, and please, no history from a textbook. Bring one object, one photograph and one thing people can eat, and tell us why those three. The students who do this well are never the ones with the most information. They are the ones who explain something small properly. Last year a student from Korea spent five minutes on a school shoe rack and it was the best table in the room. Sign-up sheet is on my door until Friday.

Hi Lais, it's Beatriz again. You asked me about the culture fair thing, so here is my honest advice. Do not try to explain Brazil. Brazil is enormous and nobody can explain it in five minutes, and if you try you will end up saying the same three sentences everybody expects. Explain your street instead. I talked about the bakery on my corner, the one that sells pao de queijo at six in the morning, and about the fact that my school year ends in December, which broke everybody's brain here. Small and specific beats big and general every single time. And take food. Take a lot of food, and you will have friends by the end of the afternoon.

extra_audio.text: Lais signs up for the culture fair table on the sheet outside the teacher's door. She chooses one object, one photograph and one thing people can eat. She writes five minutes about the street where she grew up, not about the whole country. On the day she explains why the school year in Brazil ends in December. Three people ask her questions she has never been asked before.

reading.rtitle: The Street That Explains My Country Better Than My Country Does
paras: Every exchange student is asked the same question in the first week: so, what is Brazil like? It is a question which is impossible to answer, because Brazil is a country where a four-hour flight still leaves you inside it. So I stopped answering it. Now I describe one street instead.

The street where I grew up is in Sao Paulo, in a neighbourhood which nobody outside the city has heard of. There is a bakery on the corner that opens at six in the morning, and the people who queue there at that hour are not tourists. They are the man who drives the bus, the woman who runs the flower shop, and about forty students who have not done their homework.

Two things surprise Canadians more than anything else. The first is that our school year ends in December, which means my summer holiday is their winter. The second is that a public holiday in Brazil is not the same everywhere, because a city can have holidays which belong only to that city.

The stereotype is beaches and football, and the football part is true. But the thing which is actually typical is smaller: it is a homemade cake that appears whenever more than four people are in a house, and nobody remembers who made it.

gist.prompt: What is the writer's main argument?
choices: That Brazil is impossible to visit
That describing one small, specific place explains a country better than generalising about it
That Canadians know nothing about Brazil

items: The writer stopped trying to answer the question about Brazil in general.
So I stopped answering it. Now I describe one street instead.
The people queueing at the bakery at six in the morning are tourists.
The people who queue there at that hour are not tourists.
The Brazilian school year ends in December.
Our school year ends in December, which means my summer holiday is their winter.
Public holidays are the same in every Brazilian city.
A city can have holidays which belong only to that city.

items.situation: Somebody asks: "So what is Brazil like?" Answer without generalising about the whole country.
tips: It depends on where you are.
The street where I grew up is...
It's easier if I describe one place.

items.situation: Explain to a Canadian why your summer holiday is in January.
tips: Our school year ends in December.
Christmas is a summer holiday for us.

items.situation: Somebody repeats a stereotype about Brazil that is not true. Correct it, and give a real detail instead.
tips: That's the version people see on TV.
The thing that is really typical is...

items.situation: Describe one food from home to somebody who has never seen it.
tips: It's a small cheese bread that you eat warm.
It's the thing people buy on the way to school.

items.situation: Explain what a Brazilian June party is, in three sentences, to somebody who has never heard of one.
tips: It's a party that schools organise in June.
There's food that you only eat at that time of year.
It has nothing to do with the weather, which confuses people.

items.situation: A classmate asks which Brazilian music you would put on if you had to choose one song.
tips: It depends who's in the room.
The artist that everybody my age listens to is...
I'd start with something you can dance to.
